    Hi, I'm Milagros

    Product Designer · Design Lead · Learning psychologist

    I ask why before I open Figma. Why people get stuck, why they don't adopt, why the feature should exist at all.

    How I think
    I studied how people learn before I designed anything. So I look for the moment someone gets lost, and I start there.

    Interviews, field notes, usage data. Then a prototype in code within days, in front of the people who will use it. I also write the words on the screen: years of UX writing taught me that a label can fix what a redesign can't.
    With teams

    How I design AI people can trust

    Four rules I keep in every AI product, each with the screen that proves it.

    • Gradient, for LG Ad Solutions: every change is explained and confirmed first.

      See it in Gradient →

    • The retention agent: a reason for every flag, and a draft the nurse decides on.

      See it in the retention agent →

    • Pengui: the workspace says where it runs, on the screen.

      See it in Pengui →

    • Three times the AI was wrong, and what I did

      • Court Funds

        The AIThe first approvals board let one signature release money.

        MeCourt funds need two. I rewrote the rule, the screen and the words on it.

      • Gradient

        The AIAn early draft filled missing days with averages.

        MeThe chart now marks the gap and says so before the answer.

        The AIIts first decks said "leverage" and "seamless", words the brand bans.

    How I work

    Judgment-first design, accelerated by AI.

    AI exposes the designer who only makes screens. Fast and good-looking is not the same as right.

    What AI doesWhat I decide
    Makes screens in minutesDecide what should exist
    Generates ten optionsDefine success, then pick the one that gets there
    Automates anythingJudge when automation builds trust, when it breaks it, and what never gets personalized
    Follows the promptRead what is behind it: business, users, constraints, trade-offs
    Acts the same when unsureDesign how the product behaves under uncertainty
    ExecutesOwn the problem framing, the system behavior and the decision

    The second column comes from my base in learning psychology: knowing how people think, trust and decide.

    The market does not need more interfaces. It needs better decisions about which experiences deserve to exist.

    1. Frame it

      One sentence for the problem. One person it is for. One thing they must be able to do. AI can't tell me which of those matters.

    2. Prototype

      Claude and Lovable turn the flow into something people can click, with real logic. Court Funds: seven screens from one recorded call.

    3. </>

      Design in Figma, connect to code

      Components and variables live in Figma. The Figma MCP reads them, so the prototype uses the real ones.

    4. Shipped

      Check, then ship

      A usability round, or PostHog to see where people stall. If AI drew a screen, I still read it before it goes out.

    I don't write production code: I describe, the model writes, and I read, test and ship what it wrote.

    How I lead

    I lead a team of three designers at Clear Tech. The practice didn't exist when I arrived, so I built it in three stages.

    1. Build the practice

      It did not exist, so I made it.

      ResultA skill matrix, shared frameworks, written processes and sanitized client materials the team can reuse.

    2. Connect it to the company

      Design reaches engineering and sales.

      ResultA handoff process developers follow, and prototypes and decks built with Sales and Marketing.

    3. Make it AI-competitive

      We changed how we work.

      ResultPrototypes with Claude, Lovable and the Figma MCP, and a design system anyone can use: 23 deliverables in one month, no designer needed.

    LG Ad Solutions

    Gradient: AI Analytics for Advertisers

    Brands invest millions to appear on LG smart TVs, and they all ask the same question: is it working? Gradient started with a complaint: LG's teams couldn't put data in front of advertisers like Disney or Hulu to prove it, and pulling it together by hand took hours. They asked for two things: AI, and a way to build their own dashboards. I led the product design of Gradient, the platform that came out of that brief, built mostly for LG's internal teams.

    Role
    Product Design Lead
    Team
    LG's product teams, Clear Tech's developers and me
    Year
    2025–2026
    Outcome
    Live, in use at LG
    Product
    Gradient analytics and AI agents
    Users
    LG managers and advertisers
    Reading time
    7 minutes

    Under NDA. Data, brand names and figures in these screens have been modified to protect the client.

    In 30 seconds

    The problem
    Reports took 2 to 3 days, every team had its own tools, and advertisers couldn't see if their money worked.
    What I did
    Designed one platform with the right view for each user, a marketplace where teams find and try AI agents, and a builder where an agent turns questions into dashboards.
    The result
    Gradient is live and in use by LG's teams. The platform reports that a campaign report now takes 2 seconds and that 29+ agents run in production.

    How I checked it

    Usability sessions
    Five remote sessions with LG account managers on the dashboard builder before each release, thinking aloud over a real task.
    Product analytics
    PostHog on the builder: where drafts stalled, how often Undo and "Not what I meant" were used, and which agents got a second try.
    Review set
    Real questions from LG's managers, run against every agent answer with engineering and data before release.

    The hard call

    Trust over speed. The agent could change dashboards silently and finish faster. I made it explain and confirm every change, and kept each dataset locked, because people don't use answers they don't trust.

    Why LG needed it

    LG Ad Solutions was growing faster than its operations could sustain. Gradient is the analytics side of Agentiv, the agentic platform Clear Tech built for LG: more than 29 AI agents in production, some serving clients and others running the business from the inside. Three pressures set the brief:

    • The competition was already ahead. The market had moved to automation, and fast. Nearly 1 in 4 companies were already using intelligent systems, and Meta, Google and Amazon were two or three steps ahead.
    • No one could see the ROI. Clients invested millions to appear on smart TVs, and LG could not quickly answer something basic: is it working?
    • Inefficiency was costing money. Of every dollar, only 62 cents reached mid-sized companies. Each team built its own tools, so work and spend were duplicated.

    Built in layers, with small teams

    LayerDurationPeople
    Penguiflow: the coordination8 weeks3
    Iceberg: the memory12 weeks7
    The platform: orchestration and front end20 weeks8+
    The 29+ agents, built on Agentiv32 weeks8+

    18 months of work in total, with a core team of 3 to 8 people depending on the phase.

    One platform, the right view for each user

    LG managers oversee many advertisers. Advertisers must never see each other's data. So the same screens change scope by role: managers switch clients from a selector at the top, and each client sees only its own campaigns.

    I designed a homepage for each role, because each one starts the day with a different question: account managers, team leads, company-wide leadership and external advertisers.

    • Answer first, details on demand. Headline numbers, then the trend, then proof of the value LG adds.
    • Context inside the number. Each channel card shows its own mix, so there's no extra chart to decode.
    • An assistant next to the data. Each advertiser has its own chat, so questions start from what's on screen.

    Agents people can find, trust and try

    With 29+ agents on the platform, the risk was a crowded toolbox nobody explores. In Agentiv, the platform's agent marketplace, each card does one job, explained in plain words, and one click adds or removes an agent.

    Six of the agents in the marketplace, as the platform presents them:

    For clients

    • ACR AgentLive reports

      Ask "What was my CTR in LATAM?" and get charts and an explanation.

      From 2–3 days waiting on IT to 2 seconds

    • Media Planning AgentCampaign simulation

      Projects ROI, reach and conversions before a client spends.

      See the return before investing

    • Campaign Performance AgentAutomatic monitoring

      Watches live campaigns, alerts the client when performance drops, adjusts targeting and pauses poor placements.

      Less money wasted, more conversions saved

    For LG's own teams

    • Mosaic AgentCampaign automation

      Runs setup, QA, monitoring and optimization, and catches errors before launch.

      Zero human errors, scales without friction

    • AD

      HermesAutomatic creatives

      Turns one brief into 50 to 200 ad variants by screen, region and audience.

      From 2–4 hours to 5 minutes per banner, 100× capacity

    • ROI of campaign X?

      Reporting AgentSelf-service analytics

      The team asks in Slack ("ROI of campaign X?"); it runs the queries, draws the charts and explains them in 2 seconds.

      IT freed up 25%, now on strategic projects

    A builder where AI does the work and you stay in charge

    When the standard views aren't enough, managers build their own dashboards with Gradient Agent, an AI assistant that adds charts, KPIs and filters from plain-language requests.

    The agent sets up, and explains why

    It creates one tab per dataset and says why: so charts and filters stay consistent. Every empty slot offers two paths: drag a component or ask the agent.

    Refine by chat, or by hand

    The agent confirms every change and suggests the next one. Select any chart for full control. The dataset stays locked, so data never mixes. When the agent gets a change wrong, undo takes it back, and autosave keeps the draft, so mistakes are cheap.

    Publish on purpose

    Before publishing, a dialog says exactly what will happen and who will see it, and lets you note what changed. The library then shows every dashboard's status, owner and last edit.

    The psychology behind itTrust in automation. People rely on AI the right amount when they can see what it's doing and why. So the agent never acts silently.Lee and See, 2004

    Designed for when the agent is wrong

    An agent that builds dashboards will sometimes misread a request, pick the wrong metric or answer from incomplete data. A manager who catches it once and can't fix it fast stops trusting it. So I designed the moments when it goes wrong as carefully as the ones when it goes right.

    Every change shows what it did, and undoes on its own

    Each change arrives as a card: what the agent removed and added, marked on the canvas. "Undo this change" reverts that step only, even after you've made edits of your own. "Not what I meant" shows how the agent read the request, so you correct its understanding, not just the result.

    Answers name their sources, and say what they can't stand behind

    When a manager asks why a number moved, the answer lists the dataset, dates and filters it used. If part of the data is missing or still processing, it says so first, before the answer, and the chart marks those days.

    Work you can see, and stop

    Building a dashboard takes seconds, not milliseconds. Instead of a spinner, the agent shows its plan step by step, the canvas shows where each piece will land, and Stop is always one click away. Each step is applied only when it's done.

    How we judged the agent's work

    With engineering and data, I turned real questions from LG's managers into a review set we ran before each release. Every answer had to pass four checks:

    • Right dataThe dataset, dates and filters the question implied.
    • Right numbersThe same figures as the chart built by hand.
    • Honest when unsureMissing data flagged, never filled in.
    • Never silentNo change to existing work without asking.

    Answers that failed went back into the next sprint as a design or prompt fix, and the wording of every error state came out of that review.

    Behind the screens

    It all starts with the client. We meet with LG's teams often, and the brief came out of those meetings: AI, and a way to build their own dashboards. That brief became the agent and the dashboard builder above.

    For Gradient, I first defined the product, then mapped the whole journey, then iterated on what the developers had already built.

    To move faster, we used Figma's AI agents for production work throughout the project.

    It started with a product definition

    For the dashboard builder, I first wrote down what it is and what it isn't: the pages, the flows, who owns and edits a dashboard, and what goes into the first version.

    • NavigationA dashboard library with drafts, templates, favorites and shared dashboards.
    • BuilderGrid drag and drop, resizable components, filters, tabs, undo, redo and autosave.
    • AI agentOne chat per dashboard that proposes changes, shows what they affect and can be undone.
    • PublishingDraft and published versions, sharing, ownership and collaborator permissions.

    Then the flows

    Then the iterations on what was built

    What the platform reports

    Platform metricBeforeAfter
    Create a campaign report2–3 days2 seconds
    Design an ad2–4 hours5 minutes
    Ad designs per day101,000+
    Launch a campaign2–3 weeks3–5 days
    Marketing time spent on operations60%20%
    IT time spent on reporting30%5%
    AI agents in production029+

    These are platform and engineering results as LG Ad Solutions reports them, not a measure of my design work on its own.

    What I learned

    • An AI agent needs a visible frame. Clear context, visible status and a plan step are what make people trust it.
    • Privacy has to be visible too. Permissions protect the data; clear cues about whose data you're seeing make people believe it.

    Designing for trust in AI comes down to three moves: show the plan, confirm the change and keep the data where it belongs.

    Pengui AI, a Clear Tech product

    Pengui: Agentic AI Platform

    An AI platform companies sell as their own. Pengui is Clear Tech's agentic platform: a workspace for AI agents, company knowledge and tools that runs in each client's cloud, under each client's brand. I led its product design, from the product definition with the founder to the website and the videos.

    Role
    Product Design Lead
    Year
    2025–2026
    Team
    Founder, engineers and me
    Outcome
    On the market, adopted by companies including LG
    Product
    Self-hosted, white-label AI platform
    Users
    Internal teams, and companies that resell it
    Reading time
    6 minutes

    Sample data. Names, companies and figures in these screens are fictional.

    In 30 seconds

    The problem
    Companies kept rebuilding the same pieces around every AI agent: interface, memory, permissions and monitoring.
    What I did
    Led the product design of one platform that works as an internal tool, a client-facing product and a vertical solution.
    The result
    Pengui is on the market, adopted by companies including LG, and white-label from day one.

    How I checked it

    Usability test
    The five-step setup, think-aloud, with six colleagues outside engineering: could they create a working agent without help?
    Product analytics
    PostHog on the workspace: drop-off by setup step, time to a first prompt, and how many agents got used again after a week.
    Accessibility
    Keyboard and screen-reader pass on the setup and the workspace, against WCAG.

    The hard call

    Guidance over freedom. One long form would give experts everything at once. I split it into five steps with a live summary, because Pengui is for anyone on a team, and a blank form full of options is where people give up.

    It starts with a message

    I defined the product together with the founder and the engineers. Every decision came out of our working meetings and an analysis of the business: who would buy it, who would use it, and what each of them needed to see. I was the product designer, and I also owned everything around the product: the website, its content and the videos that introduce the platform. Pengui is used internally at Clear Tech and offered to clients.

    Everything begins with a greeting and one prompt: "Write what you need and Pengui takes care of the rest."

    • Agents with a name. Each agent is a "Pengui" with one job, like a legal Pengui or an HR Pengui, so people always know who they're talking to.
    • Work, organized like teams work. Projects group conversations, scheduled work runs on its own, and a canvas holds what goes beyond a chat.
    • Every agent in one place. Teams see what each agent does, who uses it and what it's allowed to touch.

    Create a Pengui in five steps

    Anyone on a team can build an agent for their own work, no technical background needed. The empty state explains the value in three ideas, then offers one clear action: an expert in what you define, connected to your tools, shared with your team.

    The setup splits into five short steps: identity, behavior, tools, knowledge and review.

    • One decision at a time. Each step asks for a few things only, and a progress bar shows what's done and what's left.
    • A live summary on the side. The agent's name, tone, tools and files update as you go, so nothing has to be remembered.
    • Permissions, piece by piece. Tools turn on per capability (email, calendar, files, tasks), so an agent only gets the access it needs.
    • Review before creating. The last step shows everything together, with a way back to edit any part.

    Product screens in Spanish, as designed for the launch market.

    Projects keep context apart

    Projects group chats and files by topic, so a sales conversation never borrows context from a legal one. Upload up to 40 files once, from your computer or Google Drive, and reuse that knowledge in every chat of the project.

    Everything stays easy to find again: all chats live in one list with their origin (project, Pengui or general chat), and the documents agents create gather in a canvas.

    Words are part of the design

    An AI product is mostly conversation, so the microcopy carries much of the experience. A few lines from the product, and the job each one does:

    • "Escribí lo que necesitás y Pengui se encarga del resto."

      Write what you need and Pengui takes care of the rest.

      Takes away the fear of the blank prompt.

    • "¿Para qué sirve este Pengui? Una línea alcanza."

      What is this Pengui for? One line is enough.

      Makes a field feel effortless before anyone starts typing.

    • "Organizá tu trabajo con más foco y sin mezclar contextos."

      Organize your work with more focus, without mixing contexts.

      Sells the benefit, not the feature.

    • "Podés editar cualquier sección volviendo al paso correspondiente."

      You can edit any section by going back to its step.

      Makes the final step feel safe.

    Any brand, the same experience

    Clients ship agents as their own product: logo, colors, name and domain change the whole interface from one set of settings. Each client gets its own environment, and its customers never meet Pengui. There is no screen of it here: the white-label page linked below lets you pick a brand preset and watch the product change.

    The design choice: a white-label product only works if every brand looks intentional. So color, type and identity are variables in a token system, and the experience never changes.

    Control you can see

    In enterprise AI, the person who signs the contract is rarely the person who writes the prompt. Security, legal and finance always ask the same three questions, so Pengui answers them plainly:

    "Where does it run?"

    In the client's own cloud or data center.

    "What leaves our environment?"

    It depends on the models and tools the client connects, and the client chooses them.

    "Who controls access?"

    The client's administrators set identity, roles and access to agents and tools.

    Behind those answers, an admin console shows traces, activity, usage and permissions for every agent. The console isn't shown here.

    When Pengui isn't sure, or wants to act

    An agent connected to a company's email, files and calendar can do real damage with a confident wrong answer or an action nobody approved. Two patterns keep people in charge.

    Answers cite the company's own files

    Every answer drawn from a project's knowledge shows its sources, down to the page or clause. When nothing there covers the question, Pengui says so and asks before answering from general knowledge, so a guess never passes as company policy.

    It asks before it acts

    Reading is automatic; anything that sends, books or deletes stops for approval. The request shows the action, the account it uses and the draft itself, and Allow once is the default. Admins decide which tools can ever be set to always allow.

    Tested before launch

    The last step of creating a Pengui includes a test chat: its creator asks the questions their team will ask and checks the sources behind each answer before anyone else uses it.

    What I learned

    • Naming is architecture. Calling every agent a "Pengui" gave people one concept to hold, and made the whole product easier to explain and sell.
    • White label is a design-system problem first. Once color, type and identity became tokens, one product could wear any brand without breaking.
    • The buyer and the user are different people. Both need their own screen: the console for whoever signs, the workspace for whoever works.

    See Pengui live

    Pick a brand preset and watch the product change, see how it handles trust and control, or watch the platform run in short videos.

    On-Brand Without a Designer: The Clear Tech Design System

    Every deck, proposal and mock at Clear Tech used to wait for a designer. I turned the brand into a system that people and AI can both follow: foundations, components, data and AI patterns, slide and document templates, and a Claude skill that puts all of it one request away. Now anyone at the company can create on-brand presentations without designer support.

    Role
    Product Design Lead: the system, its rules, the templates and the Claude skill
    Team
    Me, with Marketing and Sales as first users
    Outcome
    Adopted company-wide
    Year
    2026
    Deliverables
    Tokens, components, AI and data patterns, slide, document and web templates, and a Claude skill
    Reading time
    5 minutes

    Sample content. Figures, names and data inside the templates are illustrative.

    In 30 seconds

    The problem
    Every deck, proposal and mock waited on a designer, and the brand lived in a PDF that no tool could read.
    What I did
    Turned the logos, the brand colors and the website into a full system, written as rules a person or a model can follow, and packaged it as a Claude skill.
    The result
    Adopted company-wide: it runs the website, the client documents and the sales proposals, and anyone creates on-brand presentations without designer support. In September 2026, people made 23 deliverables with it from the company's Claude accounts. At the four hours or more a presentation used to take a designer, that is about 90 design hours in one month.

    How I checked it

    Adoption, not opinions
    Decks, proposals and documents produced without a designer, counted month by month after the launch.
    First users
    Sales and Marketing used each release for real work and sent back what didn't fit; the rules changed from their examples.

    The hard call

    Rules over pixels. A design library would have given designers more control over every detail. I wrote the system as rules and examples that Claude can read, because the people who needed it most weren't designers, and they already worked with AI.

    From a brand guide to a system

    I started from what existed: the logos, the color pages of the brand guide and the website. From there I defined what a team needs to make something new: a palette in three tiers, DIN for headlines and Roboto for reading, a mono face for data, and spacing, corners, shadows and motion as tokens.

    Rules a model can follow

    A design system usually speaks to designers. This one also speaks to Claude. The voice has concrete rules: no "leverage" or "seamless", Title Case only for buttons, and the reader as the subject of every sentence. Each color pairing has its contrast ratio, and the tokens are written as plain values a model can read.

    Packaged as a Claude skill, the whole system loads whenever someone asks for a deck, a proposal or a mock, so the first draft already looks like Clear Tech.

    The handoff was a set of Markdown files, not a component library. I gave them to Clear Tech's director of technology, who loaded them into a Clear Tech agent that adapts content to the brand automatically. The system now works without me, or anyone, in the loop for a first draft.

    Variables in Figma

    The system's decisions live as Figma variables: each semantic color has a light and a dark value and a name that says what it is for, like color/brand/primary. When I prototype with Claude, the Figma MCP reads those variables straight from the file, so the prototype uses the real values and a change in Figma shows up in the next prototype.

    There is no tokens file in a product codebase: the handoff was the Markdown and the skill. For tokens handed to developers, see the Biomás app.

    Patterns for a data and AI company

    Clear Tech sells data and AI, so the system covers what that work looks like on screen: an AI chat that cites its sources, an agent trace that shows each step, confidence labels on forecasts, pipeline status and KPI cards.

    Templates for selling

    Most of what the company produces is meant to sell: decks, proposals and the website. The system includes ten slide layouts, document and email templates, engagement tiers and a website kit, so a salesperson starts from a finished page, not a blank one.

    The system in use

    The system doesn't live in a folder. It runs the Clear Tech website, its client documents and its sales proposals, all from the same tokens, components and voice.

    My favorite piece is Success Stories, a 15-page document with four client cases. Each one leads with the client and the problem, then what was built and the results, so a reader can compare them at a glance.

    See it live

    The Clear Tech website runs on this system.

    clear-tech.com (opens in a new tab)

    What I learned

    • The users of a design system aren't only designers. Here most of them sell, and they work alongside a model.
    • Rules need examples. A model, like a person, follows "don't say leverage" better with an on-brand line right next to it.
    • Say what you inferred. The system marks what came from the brand guide and what I defined, so anyone can check it.

    The test of a design system: anyone can use it without asking a designer.

    Changent, a Clear Tech proposal

    A Human-in-the-Loop Retention Agent for Home-Visit Nurses

    Changent already owned a model that flags the clients most likely to leave its home-visiting program. The flag rarely turned into action. I designed the layer around it: an agent that shows each nurse who needs action today and why, drafts an approach the nurse decides on, and gives supervisors the same data aggregated. Then I built the prototype and rebuilt the Phase 2 proposal around it.

    Role
    Product Design Lead: research, story, content and prototype
    Team
    Clear Tech's data experts and me
    Outcome
    Phase 2 approved
    Year
    2026
    Deliverables
    Two proposals and a working prototype with nurse and supervisor views
    Reading time
    5 minutes

    Under NDA. Names, data and figures in this case have been modified to protect the client, and all prototype data is synthetic.

    In 30 seconds

    The problem
    An accurate model, a flag that rarely turned into action, and a 10-slide proposal that asked for a yes on slide 2, before proving anything.
    What I did
    Shaped the agent with the Clear Tech experts who know the client, designed the nurse and supervisor views as a working prototype, and rebuilt the proposal around it.
    The result
    Phase 2 approved. The room went from "what is this for?" to "when can we start?"

    How I checked it

    Expert walkthroughs
    Every part of the prototype reviewed one by one with the Clear Tech experts who work with Changent's data.
    What comes first in Phase 2
    A usability test with nurses on the priority list and the "Why it flagged" panel, before anything is built.
    Measurement
    12-week retention and days from flag to first contact, nurses with the agent against nurses without, over one quarter.

    The hard call

    Proof before the ask. The original asked for a yes on slide 2. I moved the ask to the end, after the evidence and the demo, because a room that agrees with the diagnosis says yes on its own.

    Where I started

    The flag from Changent's model landed in a weekly report and rarely turned into action. The Phase 2 proposal meant to fix that was ten slides with the same layout: no numbers from the model, a product told in bullets, a yes requested on slide 2. Nobody had seen a single screen.

    Before touching a screen or a slide, I met one by one with the Clear Tech experts who work with Changent every day, shaped the proposal with them and later validated every part of the prototype with them. That is also the limit of the research: it went through Clear Tech's domain experts, who know Changent's data first-hand, not through nurses or supervisors. Three insights changed the pitch:

    • Nurses don't need to know who is at risk; they need to know what to do.
    • The report competes with a full visit schedule, and loses.
    • The model is accurate, but it never learns from what happens next.

    So the message changed from "let's build an agent" to "you already own an engine that works; what's missing is everything around it." An easier yes: nobody has to admit they were wrong. The deck only said the model "works"; I went and got the numbers:

    1 in 3
    flagged clients actually left, vs about 1 in 8 of everyone else
    ~100 days
    between the first flag and drop-out: three months to act
    57%
    of upcoming drop-outs sat inside the riskiest 30%

    What the agent does, and never does

    Two components, one circuit. The prediction engine is the one Changent already owns; the recommendation layer is new, and reads Changent's own guidance to match it to each case. The engine flags a client, the agent alerts the right nurse, explains why and drafts a plan, and the nurse acts with the client. The nurse is the decision point, every time.

    Five decisions carry that promise through the prototype:

    • A priority list, not a report. Each nurse opens on who needs action today, ranked by risk, with the trend next to every name. Risk rising for two or more weeks precedes most drop-outs, so it gets its own count at the top.
    • Every flag explains itself. A "Why it flagged" panel says in plain words what changed: contact thinned to text only, two visits missed in a row, the pattern of families who leave the program.
    • The agent drafts; the nurse decides. The suggested approach arrives as a draft, matched to Changent's own guidance and ready to edit. The nurse reviews, adapts and decides; the agent never acts without the nurse.
    • It learns from what happens next. In Phase 2 the model logs every outcome and tracks each client's risk trend, rising or falling and why, instead of a one-shot weekly snapshot.
    • Supervisors see the same data, aggregated. Flags acted on by nurse, median days from flag to first contact, and 12-week retention for the team.

    Open the live prototype (opens in a new tab)Nurse and manager views, with synthetic data.

    Who sees what

    This is health information, so I designed it under HIPAA rules and got HIPAA-certified for the project. The two views are not two layouts of the same data: each role gets the minimum it needs to do its job, and every time the agent or a person touches a client record, it is logged.

    That view is also the measurement plan: 12-week retention and time from flag to first contact, compared between nurses who use the agent and nurses who don't, over one quarter.

    The proposal: proof before the ask

    Then I rebuilt the deck around the prototype. The original asked for a yes on slide 2. I moved the ask to the end, gave the model's numbers a screen of their own, and replaced the bullets about a future product with the working prototype, opened live from a slide.

    The original deck: correct, but static.

    A room pays attention, understands, remembers and only then decides, so the deck was built in that order: the proof alone on a screen, two named components instead of five loose steps, the live demo as the peak, an easy ask as the end, and "the nurse decides" said before anyone could object.

    The psychology behind itIdentifiable victim effect. The prototype follows Avery, case #48, not "the riskiest 30%". A room remembers one person; it forgets a percentage.Small and Loewenstein, 2003

    The deck I presented

    I designed this deck for the meeting with the client in the United States, where Phase 2 was approved. Six of its screens, in order:

    Client logo blurred. Figures in these screens have been modified.

    A second proposal: App and AI Innovation

    The team took a second proposal to the US, and I designed that one too: one app built around the nurse, that captures paper forms with AI and acts on retention risk. For the same client I also designed a dashboard with its guides, in Dashboards People Adopt.

    The result

    Phase 2 was approved. The conversation went from "what is this for?" to "when can we start?"

    What weighed most, in order: the evidence screen, the live prototype, and not asking for anything until the room agreed with the diagnosis.

    What I'd test next. Whether nurses read "flags acted on, by nurse" as support or as surveillance. The prototype words it as a prompt for a conversation; only nurses can tell me if it lands that way.

    This is where I learned that the order of a story decides its ending.

    Court Funds Platform Prototype + Proposal

    Selling a platform before it existed. A bank needed a system for court-administered funds: more than 100,000 accounts running on paper and spreadsheets. After one discovery call, I designed the proposal and a seven-screen prototype that made it safe to say yes.

    Role
    Product Design Lead: discovery, narrative, proposal and prototype
    Team
    With the co-founder and Head of Marketing
    Outcome
    Deal closed; the account is active today
    Year
    2026
    Deliverable
    A 10-section proposal and an interactive prototype
    Reading time
    3 minutes

    Under NDA. The client's name and branding were removed, and data and figures in these screens have been modified.

    In 30 seconds

    The problem
    Banks don't buy promises, least of all for systems that move court-ordered money. And there was nothing to see yet.
    What I did
    Turned one recorded call into a 10-section proposal and a seven-screen prototype. I set the flows, the rules and the words; AI produced the screens; I checked each one against how court funds work.
    The result
    The bank signed, and the account is active today.

    The hard call

    De-risk over impress. A flashier pitch was possible. I put what we wouldn't build next to what we would, and showed the price only after the prototype, because this buyer couldn't afford to be wrong.

    My brief: make "yes" feel safe

    This buyer couldn't afford to be wrong. So every section and screen had to answer two questions:

    What does the buyer need to believe next?

    What makes believing that effortless?

    • Diagnose before prescribing. I gave them their own problem, in their words, stated more precisely than they had stated it to us.
    • Make the invisible tangible. A described platform asks the buyer to imagine it. A prototype does the imagining for them.

    The psychology behind itLoss aversion. For a bank, a bad decision hurts far more than a good one helps. So every screen answered "what could go wrong?" before anyone asked.Kahneman and Tversky, 1979

    One conversation, ten sections

    The co-founder and the Head of Marketing led the commercial conversation. I worked from the recorded call: researched how court funds work, and turned what the bank had told us into a story the buyer could walk down, one doubt at a time.

    1. Need
    2. Diagnosis
    3. Vision
    4. Scope
    5. Technology
    6. See it working
    7. How we work
    8. Team
    9. Investment
    10. Why us

    Trust you can see

    In banking and justice, trust is the product. So the prototype made every rule visible.

    Money can only reach the right person

    Each account is locked to its beneficiary's tax ID at creation, and the form says so in plain words.

    Two signatures, zero informality

    Every request shows its signature progress, 1 of 2 or 2 of 2, and every action lands in an audit log.

    Each team sees its part

    Court operators see their own case files; the central authority sees every fund. The client's org chart, built into the navigation.

    The result

    The bank signed, and the account is active today.

    From one recorded call: a 10-section proposal, a seven-screen prototype, and the platform's rules made visible on the screens. The engineers will build it from the prototype that sold it.

    What I learned

    • In regulated industries, trust is the feature. Every screen that answered "what could go wrong?" was worth more than one that showed what the product could do.
    • A prototype is a sales argument that can't be misread. It ended the "imagine that…" part of the conversation.

    What I'd test next: the approvals flow, with real court operators, before anything is built.

    A prototype can close a deal before a single line of code exists. This one did.

I led a co-design workshop where the CEO, the Growth Director and the brokers built one scoreboard together, and the design of the dashboard that came out of it, delivered in Power BI, with a UX designer on my team.

    Role
    Product Design Lead
    Team
    UX designer, business analyst, data specialist and PM
    Outcome
    Delivered in Power BI
    Method
    Co-design workshop
    Reading time

    Confidential. The client's name and logo were removed, and names, offices and figures in these screens are fictional.

    The dashboard is in Spanish. "Tablero Master" is the master dashboard, "Facturación total" total revenue, "Operaciones cerradas" closed deals, "Nuevas captaciones" new listings and "Cartera activa" active portfolio.

    The problem

    The hard call

    With them, not for them. Designing the dashboard ourselves would have been faster. We built it with the brokers instead, because a scoreboard people help create is one they actually use.

    We didn't bring a solution. We built one with them.

    Instead of designing a dashboard and asking for approval, we ran a co-design workshop with the people who would use it: the CEO, the Growth Director and brokers from different zones.

    1. Listen

      Interviews with brokers and advisors: the problems as they live them, not as head office assumes them.

    2. Sketch

    3. Test

      Prototypes shown back, feedback collected and the design refined until it fit.

    2. 4

      Client contacts, offers, property visits and reports sent.

    3. 4

      Reservations

      Active and canceled, in count and in value.

    4. 6

      Closing

      Closed deals, publication time, portfolio turnover and commissions.

    It all lands in the dashboard at the top of this page, where each role sees what it needs: the CEO sees the network, a broker sees the office, an agent sees their own numbers. It opens inside the client's own platform, with single sign-on.

    Two modules the brokers asked for

    One question, before and after

    Monday morning, the CEO asks: which office converted best last quarter, and why?

    What was delivered

    • 21 shared metrics in four stages, agreed by the CEO, the Growth Director and the brokers.
    • One Power BI dashboard inside the client's own platform, with single sign-on and a view for the CEO, for brokers and for agents.
    • Two modules the brokers asked for: client management and employee management.
    • A long-term plan and documentation.

    They got what they never had: a way to compare their offices.

    What I learned

    • Adoption starts in the workshop, not at launch. The brokers who wrote the metrics defended the dashboard before it existed.
    • Shared definitions beat clever charts. Agreeing on what a "lead" means did more for the network than any visualization.

    Global tech company, under NDA

    Workforce Reduction Platform Prototype

    From spreadsheets to a consistent, auditable flow. Workforce reductions are among the hardest decisions a company makes. This client ran them on manual spreadsheets, where one wrong formula has a human and legal cost. I designed a prototype that makes every step consistent, explained and ready for audit.

    Role
    Sole designer, end to end
    Deliverable
    Interactive prototype
    Users
    HR leaders, managers and downstream teams
    Reading time
    3 minutes

    Under NDA. The client's name and branding were removed, and all names, data and figures have been modified.

    The problem
    Counts, scores and names were handled by hand in spreadsheets, in a process where every mistake hurts people and creates legal risk.
    What I did
    Designed five guided steps with locked logic, automatic calculations and mandatory reasons for every exception.
    The result
    A prototype where every decision is consistent and explained, plus one master roster all downstream teams can act on.

    The hard call

    Good friction. Most flows remove friction. Here I added it on purpose, with written reasons for exceptions and a deliberate stop before locking, because some decisions should be slow.

    Five steps, one decision at a time

    A process that lived across tabs, formulas and emails became one guided path. Each step unlocks only when the previous one is complete.

    1. Project setup

      A locked project name for all documentation, dates and the organizational scope, picked from a tree.

    2. Business case

      Elimination or re-org, a legal justification, and filters that count impacted employees automatically.

    3. Scoring logic

      Weighted criteria that must add up to 100%, with tenure as the tie-breaker.

    4. Selection roster

      A ranked list where managers decide, and explain any exception before submitting.

    5. Executive summary

      Headcount, savings and before and after by organizational unit, in one view.

    Exceptions explained, decisions recorded

    In a process this sensitive, the interface asks for a reason at every exception and leaves a trail an audit can follow.

    • Exceptions need a reason. Keeping a low-ranked employee or letting go of a high-ranked one requires a written justification.
    • Logic you can't change quietly. Each scoring setup is versioned and locked, so every result can be traced back to its rules.
    • A final check before locking. The roster submits only when every employee has a decision and every required reason is written, and then it's recorded with time and user.

    One roster, every team

    After the notification, the product produces one master roster of the affected employees. Every team that has to act works from the same list:

    • CompensationCalculates severance and final payments
    • LegalPrepares the separation documents to sign
    • BenefitsExtends health coverage through COBRA
    • IT supportDeactivates user accounts
    • SecurityDeactivates access badges

    What I'm improving now

    A first version is a starting point. Walking through the flow, I found three places where people still had to think too hard, or could make a mistake they couldn't take back.

    • Suggested weightsReady-made weight sets, so nobody has to do the math in their head. They can still adjust them.
    • A clear stop before lockingOnce submitted, the roster locks for audit and can't be changed, so a final dialog summarizes the decision and its consequences.
    • Saved progress and datesEvery step saves its state and shows its start and closing date, because each stage of the process has a deadline.

    Next on the list

    • Numbers that agreeThe roster, the confirmation dialog and the executive summary don't yet show the same counts. Next is making every screen tell the same story.
    • "Not retained", not "Eliminate"The roster's decision button becomes "Not retained". In a flow like this, the word matters.
    • An adverse-impact review before lockingThe flow requires a reason for every exception and records who decided what, but it doesn't yet check whether the selection falls harder on any group. That review comes before the lock.

    What changes

    TaskBeforeWith the prototype
    Count impacted employeesManual counting in spreadsheetsAutomatic, from filters
    Score and rankManual formulasVersioned, locked logic
    Explain exceptionsScattered across files and emailsRequired, and saved in the audit trail
    Hand off to other teamsA spreadsheet per teamOne master roster

    A hard process can't be made easy. It can be made clear, consistent and accountable.

    Some friction is a feature: here, the slow parts of the flow are the point.

    Biomás

    Biomás Donor Collection App

    A field app for a nationwide network. Biomás collects donations at donors' homes in 18 of Argentina's 24 provinces; the donations become fertility treatments. I led the product strategy of the native app its collectors and field reps use every day: I defined the features, validated them with stakeholders and approved every screen a junior designer produced in Figma. I also wrote and designed its quick-start guides and Play Store page.

    Role
    Product Design Lead
    Product
    Native app, web app, quick-start guides and Play Store page
    Users
    Collectors and field reps
    Reading time
    3 minutes

    Early version. These screens come from the first version of the app, and all donor names and data are fictional.

    The problem
    Routes were planned by hand, donor data was unreliable, and field reps wrote everything twice: on paper, then in a web app.
    What I did
    Led the product strategy of one native app for two kinds of users, approved every screen a junior designer produced, and wrote the quick-start guides that taught people to use it.
    The result
    One app for the whole network, in use across the country. The client bought the guides as an extra.

    The hard call

    Street first, not desk first. It would have been easy to squeeze the web app onto a phone. My call: design for the street instead. Offline by default, scan before you type and one main action per screen, because this work happens in trucks and doorways, by outsourced collectors who are not tech-savvy.

    How I framed the problem

    Field reps visit donors at home. With no app, they filled in a paper form at the door and typed it all again into a web app back at the office: double work, late data and copying errors on records the final product's quality depends on.

    Where the learning came from. I did not go to the field myself. Our PM did: she went out with field reps and talked with them about their rounds. I worked from her notes, the business requirements and the PRD, and checked each decision back with her and the client's stakeholders.

    Three things from the field set the brief:

    • No signal, often. Many homes are in areas with poor coverage, so nothing could depend on a connection.
    • No time at the door. A rep stands in a doorway, sometimes in areas where holding a phone out for long is not safe. Registering a donor had to take seconds.
    • One entry, not two. Whatever replaced the paper form had to be the record itself, not a draft to retype later.

    What I ruled out.

    • The web app on a phone. The fastest to ship, but it needed signal and kept forms built for a desk.
    • A full-featured app. Everything the web app did, in the pocket. Too much to learn and too slow to use on a doorstep.
    • What we built instead. A small native app that does a few things: offline by default, few fields, one main action per screen. Management keeps the heavy work in the web app.

    The result of that call is the number that matters most here: data entry went from two steps to one.

    Two users, one app

    Collectors

    Plan the day's route, follow it on the map and scan each container to link the sample to its donor.

    Field reps

    Register donors without signal, edit or remove them, add photos and each home's location, and get alerts about duplicates.

    Three calls from that first version still hold up: a status on every donor, directions with a landmark, and a way out when a code won't scan.

    Built for the street

    • Works without signal. Everything is saved offline and syncs when the connection comes back.
    • Fast and safe to open. Biometric login, so no one types a password on a doorstep.
    • Everyone in the loop. Push notifications for the team, and WhatsApp for donors: welcome messages, complaints, cancellations and address changes.

    The psychology behind itSituational impairments. On the street, with one hand busy and little attention to spare, everyone has less capacity. So the main actions are big, scanning replaces typing, and nothing depends on signal.Sears et al., 2003

    Behind the screens

    Every flow, state and component was worked out in Figma before any screen was polished; the junior designer produced the boards and I approved each one.

    Tokens before screens

    Color is named by what it means, not by how it looks. Each status has a role color and a background to pair it with (Error BG, Warning BG, Info BG, Success), so a status reads the same on the donor list, in a message and on a button. The components sit on top of those roles and follow Material, the native Android kit the developers built with, so what they received matched what they already had in code.

    Role, as named in FigmaValueUsed for
    Error#B50E0EErrors and actions that cannot be undone
    Advertencia#AB4905Warnings that need a look before going on
    Información#1365BBNeutral notices and the main action
    Íconos#6D7599Icons and secondary marks

    Values read from the component sheet above, from the first version of the app.

    Guides that helped people adopt it

    A new app in the street only works if people learn it fast. With my background in learning design, I created quick-start guides for collectors and for field reps: I researched what each one needed, wrote every page and designed them to be read standing on a sidewalk.

    The Play Store page

    The store screenshots follow the same idea: one benefit per screen, for each kind of user.

    The result

    In use across the network, in 18 of Argentina's 24 provinces. The client bought the quick-start guides as an extra.

    The work stayed in the street. The paperwork didn't.

    What I'd change today

    • Bigger targetsThe three-dot menus are small for someone holding a container. I'd make the whole row tappable.
    • Status beyond colorColored pills with thin borders fade in sunlight. I'd add icons and stronger contrast.
    • One main actionScan, deregister and complaint look equal. Scanning should lead, and deregistering should ask for confirmation.
    • Visible syncOffline mode only helps if people trust it. I'd show what's saved and what's still waiting to sync.

    The street set the brief: busy hands and days that don't go as planned.

    Dashboards People Adopt: Power BI Standards and Guides

    One look and feel for every dashboard. Many teams were building and updating Power BI dashboards, each in its own way. I led a 96-page UX guide and set of standards for every team building them: I defined its sections from the client's needs and supervised its design. For the rollout of the new dashboards, I also designed a two-page cheat sheet.

    Role
    Product Design Lead
    Year
    2024
    Deliverables
    A 96-page UX guide and standards, plus a two-page rollout cheat sheet
    Reading time
    3 minutes

    Confidential. The client's name, logo and internal tools were removed from these pages.

    The problem
    Every team built dashboards its own way, so the same company looked and behaved differently from one report to the next.
    What I did
    Defined the sections from the client's needs, supervised the design of one guide covering brand, components, layout, data visualization and accessibility, and designed the cheat sheet for the rollout.
    The result
    One standard for every dashboard: a reference anyone can follow to build a consistent, accessible dashboard, without a designer in the room.

    The hard call

    Rules with reasons. A list of specs would have been faster to write. My call: every rule comes with its why and a real example, because people follow guidance they understand and ignore rules they don't.

    What's inside

    Ninety-six pages of UX guidance and standards for every team building Power BI dashboards: brand foundations first, then each component, then the patterns that tie them together. Two pages at full size, then an overview of three more. Further down, the same approach for another client, Changent: a dashboard, its training guide and a release guide.

    Data and accessibility, made practical

    Beyond the components, the guide teaches how to choose the right chart for each question and how to check that everyone can read it, with step-by-step examples.

    The psychology behind itWorked examples. People learn a rule faster from a solved example than from a definition. So every rule in the guide comes with one.Sweller and Cooper, 1985

    A cheat sheet for the rollout

    A new dashboard only helps if people know how to use it. To support the rollout of the new Power BI dashboards, I also designed a two-page cheat sheet: every navigation feature, from exporting and sharing to bookmarks and filters, explained right next to where it appears on screen.

    For Changent: a dashboard and its guides

    The same approach for another client. For Changent, I designed an internal Power BI dashboard for its program teams: a side-by-side comparison of two programs across referrals, service delivery and outcomes, for supervisors, nursing practice managers and network management. Then the part most dashboards skip: as part of the product strategy, I led the training guide and the communication material so people would actually adopt it.

    The same for Changent's Fidelity reports: a redesigned 3.0 version with the element name up top, filters in a logical order, a status badge that says "at target" or "below target" at a glance, a legend before the charts and plain-language outcomes in the details view. And a one-page release guide so every change made sense to the people reading it.

    What I learned

    • A rule without a reason gets skipped. So every rule in the guide comes with its why and a real example, not just a spec.
    • The best guide works without me in the room. If a guide needs its author to be understood, it isn't finished.
    • Accessibility sticks when it's three steps. Instead of a policy, the guide gives a tool, a number to meet and a failing example, so anyone can run the check.
    • Onboarding is part of the product. A dashboard nobody knows how to read is a dashboard nobody uses, so the rollout got its own deliverable: the cheat sheet.

    This is where I learned to write rules people actually follow: with a reason and an example.

    CAMMESA Agent Portal Prototype

    CAMMESA settles who gets paid for the electricity Argentina used: 95% of the country's electricity goes through its system. While its settlement engine was being rebuilt one process at a time, the market's agents needed a new portal, because the old one ran on outdated technology. I set the product strategy and directed the design; a designer on my team produced the screens with AI tools. Version 1 went to the client marked ready for development, and the portal is now being built.

    Role
    Product Design Lead: direction and product strategy
    Team
    A designer from my team, with me directing and giving feedback
    Outcome
    Prototype delivered, in development
    Users
    Market agents who report readings, and CAMMESA's teams
    Reading time
    3 minutes

    Demo data. Files, agents and meters in these screens are demo values, not real market data.

    The problem
    Agents reported their readings through a portal built on outdated technology, with no way to see whether a file arrived, why it was rejected or what was missing.
    What I did
    Set the product strategy and directed the design from the client's request to dev-ready screens, giving feedback at every round to the designer on my team who produced them with AI tools.
    The result
    A dev-ready prototype, now in development: emergency uploads, file history, missing measurements, rejections with their reason and automatic claims. CAMMESA's early feedback: positive.

    The hard call

    Boring on purpose. The agents are utilities and generators reporting data that decides who gets paid. My call: a plain, conventional interface over anything clever. Familiar patterns, a status on every file and the reason for every rejection, because in a system that moves a market's money, surprise is a defect.

    Why the stakes were high

    The system behind the portal settles 95% of Argentina's electricity. Its engine was migrated one process at a time, each one run side by side with the original until every number matched: a team of four, twelve months from first meeting to stage 1 delivered. A settlement error here isn't a typo; it's a payment to the wrong company, across an entire market. The portal was the part the market would actually see.

    Where it started

    The brief came as a list and a few screenshots: five screens to mock up, a menu based on the old portal, and the old portal itself, which told us everything about what not to repeat.

    Five moments in an agent's month, before and now

    We designed around what an agent actually goes through: a reading that misses the normal run, a file that may or may not have arrived, a rejection, a gap nobody noticed, and CAMMESA chasing what's missing. Each one got its screen, shown below as a before-and-now board; open a board to see it larger.

    The psychology behind itVisibility of system status. People trust a system that tells them what's happening. Every file has a status, every rejection its reason, every gap its own view.Nielsen, 1994

    Directed, not drawn

    This one I didn't draw. I set the strategy and defined what each screen had to answer; the designer on my team explored, built and iterated the screens with AI tools, and I gave feedback at every round. My call: treat the client's list of five screens as five moments in an agent's month, and design each screen around its moment. Version 1 went to the client marked ready for development; the current version is what the engineers are building.

    What I learned

    • Direction is a deliverable. A clear strategy, a question for every screen and feedback at every round let a designer on my team take a portal for a national market from a client's list to dev-ready screens, with AI tools to move faster.
    • In high-stakes systems, clarity beats cleverness. The best compliment this portal can get is that nobody noticed it.
    • The number to watch. Once the portal is live: how many rejected files get re-uploaded correctly within an hour, now that agents see the reason.

    Leading design here meant not touching every pixel: set the strategy, ask the right questions and let the team build.

    ClimatePath: From Emissions Data to a Plan a City Can Defend

    Thousands of cities have a greenhouse gas inventory. Far fewer have a plan they are delivering. I wanted to know why, so I designed and built ClimatePath: three questions, one screen each, that take a city's emissions data and walk a sustainability officer to a prioritized action plan they can put in front of a council. Underneath is one idea: estimates the officer can argue with, and an AI draft that shows what it was given.

    Open the live prototype (opens in a new tab) Jump to how it works

    Three minutes: the picture below, element by element and the hypotheses. Eleven minutes: everything.

    Role
    Sole designer, end to end
    Type
    Self-initiated concept
    Platform
    Web, responsive, light and dark
    Prototype
    Working, built with Claude
    Reading time
    4 minutes, 11 with the full case

    Self-initiated. No client, no brief, no users yet. The cities are fictional and the emission factors are illustrative, so validation and metrics are written as what I would do, with the hypotheses and the criteria spelled out, not as results. The 30-minute path from inventory to brief is a design target, not a measurement.

    The problem
    A city's inventory is produced for reporting and then sits in a folder. Which actions get funded is decided in meetings by what is politically easy, and justifying the choice to council takes weeks.
    What I did
    Framed the problem around one person, set four principles, and built a working prototype with AI in two weeks: three steps where every screen moves the user toward a decision.
    The result
    A live tool on an existing open-source design system, designed so an officer can get from inventory to a council brief in under 30 minutes (a target, still to be tested), with a validation and measurement plan ready to run.

    The hard call

    Decisions, not dashboards. The obvious product was a comprehensive emissions dashboard: every sector, every year, every chart. I cut all of it. If a chart doesn't change what the officer does next, it doesn't ship. The bet is that a tool that gets one person to one defensible decision is worth more than one that shows everyone everything.

    The gap between a report and a decision

    The inventory exists. The decision doesn't. ClimatePath lives in the gap between them.

    More than 10,000 cities have committed to climate targets. Reading their public plans and inventories, the same story repeats: the inventory exists, the plan doesn't. ClimatePath covers the stretch where the chain breaks, from prioritizing to justifying.

    The person at the center

    A sustainability officer in a city of 50,000 to 500,000. Often a team of one. Not a data scientist. Measured on whether things get done, not on how the report looks.

    Needs: know where to focus, defend the choice to elected officials, do it without an analyst.
    Frustrations: data that doesn't point to decisions; pressure to show progress with no clear path.

    How might we

    …turn an emissions inventory into a prioritized action plan a sustainability officer can defend, without an analyst?

    Out of scope on purpose: calculating the inventory (other tools do it), tracking delivery over time, anything that needs data most cities don't have.

    Built to be argued with

    Every number shows its assumption. The AI writes only from numbers the officer chose, and calls itself a draft.

    The product rests on one bet: an officer will defend a plan they can see through and change. Two things make that possible.

    Estimates you can argue with. Each action is a dot. Hover it and you get the basis of the estimate, the cost and the rollout time. Drag it to disagree, and a dotted ghost stays where it was. Every card in the brief carries its assumption: “cuts about 35% of waste emissions at full rollout; illustrative; adjust with local data.”

    A draft, not a verdict. Claude drafts the council brief from the plan's own numbers, under three rules: it only receives what the officer already saw; it must mark estimates; every output shows its assumptions. A note under the draft says so in plain words, and the officer signs a checklist before presenting. When someone in the room says “an AI wrote this,” the answer is short: it wrote only the rationale, from numbers the officer chose and can edit, and a person signed it off.

    Try the matrix here. Click a dot to add it to the plan. Drag it to disagree with the estimate. Target: 270,000 t.
    0 t / yr
    Nothing selected yet.

    The psychology behind itOwnership. People value what they helped shape. An officer who adjusted three estimates and saved two scenarios will defend that plan in a way they would never defend a printout. Dragging a dot isn't a gimmick; it's how the plan becomes theirs.Norton, Mochon and Ariely, 2012

    The full case

    The principles, every step of the tool, the edge states, how it sits on an existing design system, and how I'd validate and measure it.

    Read the full case7 more minutes

    Four principles that settled every argument

    Four rules written before any screen. Each one killed a feature I liked.

    1. Decisions, not dashboardsIf a chart doesn't change what the user does next, it doesn't ship. Killed: the year-by-year sector trend view.
    2. Show your workEvery number shows the assumption behind it, so the user can challenge it. Killed: the clean “AI-generated plan” with no assumptions.
    3. Good enough beats perfectRough estimates with visible ranges beat no estimate. Killed: waiting for perfect emission factors before testing.
    4. Built for the council meetingThe output must survive a room of non-experts. Killed: an export to CSV instead of a printable brief.

    Fourteen days, in order. Two days reading public climate plans and inventory standards, synthesized with Claude and verified by hand against their sources. Two days on these principles, the non-goals and the three-step flow in Figma. Three days building with Claude as a pair of hands: delegate a piece, review it against the principles, cut what didn't serve them. Three days using it as the officer would, on a laptop and a phone. Four days fixing what that showed: undo, quick wins, best next action, keyboard access.

    How it works, element by element

    Three steps, one question each. Every element is there for a reason.

    Hover or tap a number to read what each element is and why it's there.

    Step 1 · Where does our carbon come from?

    1. The question, not the feature. Each step's title is what the officer is asking, so the screen reads as an answer.
    2. Emissions as a flow, not a pie. Ribbons converge into one total. The two thickest answer “where do we focus” before any text does.
    3. Total next to per-person. 900,000 tonnes means nothing; 5.0 per person next to a 3–6 benchmark means something.
    4. Start from a sample city. A blank form is where people leave. Pick a similar city and edit; typing your own numbers is one option away.
    5. The commitment, not progress. The gauge shows −30% by 2030. Progress belongs in step two, once there's a plan to measure.

    Step 2 · What could we actually do?

    1. Plain-language quadrants. “Quick wins · do first” tells a first-timer where to start without reading the axes.
    2. One dot, four encodings. Position is impact and effort, size is cost, colour is sector, the same colours as the city's inventory tool. Click to add; drag to disagree.
    3. The plan, live. Projected reduction against the target updates with every click: the number the council will ask about, always a glance away.
    4. Tonnes become cars. “About 61,500 cars off the road for a year.” Rounded, so it reads as an estimate. This is the line that gets quoted in the meeting.
    5. Trajectory to 2030. Each action has a rollout time, so the line bends toward the target instead of dropping at once. “Are we there yet” without reading a number.

    Step 3 · How do we explain it to council?

    1. A document, not a screen. Cover, date, audience. It looks like what gets handed around a council room, because that's where it has to win.
    2. Four numbers a councillor remembers. Tonnes, share of target, cost, number of actions. Everything else is detail.
    3. AI drafts from the plan's own numbers. The model only receives what the user already saw. The status line says so, and shows “Drafting 2 of 5” while it works.
    4. A draft, not a verdict. The note under the draft says it in plain words.
    5. Every card carries its assumptions. Sector, tonnes, and the basis of the estimate underneath, so each line can be challenged.

    Designed to guide: the edge states

    An officer opens this once, under pressure, with a meeting on the calendar. The edge states are designed on purpose.

    • Coming back. The plan is saved in the browser: resume where you left off, or start fresh. This gets built between meetings, not in one go.
    • Never a blank panel. No actions? “Add the quick wins.” Some? The best next action by tonnes per dollar. Help sits behind “how to read this,” closed until needed.
    • Mistakes are cheap. Removing an action gives you Undo. You can't move to step two with an empty inventory; the button waits and the first field gets focus.
    • Works with a finger and a keyboard. Dots are 44px targets. Every dot is focusable, toggles with Enter, and arrow keys adjust the estimate for anyone who can't drag. On a phone, the matrix scrolls sideways and a floating dock keeps the total in view.

    Inside an existing design system

    Adopted an open-source city design system, then fixed where it fails.

    A tool for cities shouldn't look like a startup landing page. I adopted the design tokens of CityCatalyst, an open-source platform cities use to build their inventories: brand blues, navy content, the five official sector colours, 8 and 16px radii, Poppins and Open Sans. An officer moving from their inventory tool into ClimatePath shouldn't feel they changed products.

    Adopting a system also means checking it, and deciding where to depart:

    DecisionWhat the system doesWhat I did, and why
    Colour budgetBrand blue on headings, numbers and tinted backgrounds60-30-10: neutral canvas, white cards with 1px borders, blue only on actions and focus. Blue on blue was tiring to read.
    Sector colours III, IV, V2.4:1, 2.0:1 and 1.8:1 on light surfaces; below the 3:1 for non-text UIKept for consistency with the inventory tool, added a navy outline to every dot, never let colour carry meaning alone. Flagged for the system's owners.
    Dark modeLight onlyDerived dark values from the same navy and blue scale; edge lighting instead of glow; the brief's cover stays navy in both modes.
    Token namescolors.brand.500, colors.sector.ISame path in Figma (color/brand/primary) and in code (--accent, --s-energy), so a developer finds the match without a mapping document.

    Accessibility checked, not claimed: text contrast 14.8:1 and 6.4:1 on brand; full keyboard operation with visible focus; 44px targets; names and roles on every control; reduced-motion respected. Still open: a full screen-reader pass of the matrix.

    How I'd validate it

    Four hypotheses written to fail, three stages, a go criterion at each.

    H1

    Officers trust an estimate once they can see the assumption

    Test: think-aloud with and without the tooltip and the assumption line.
    Fails if: participants still say “where does this come from” after seeing it.

    H2

    The matrix is the moment it clicks

    Test: ask participants to explain the plan to a colleague after 10 minutes.
    Fails if: they reach for the list instead of the matrix, or can't name a trade-off.

    H3

    Nobody wants to upload a file

    Test: offer upload, paste and “start from a similar city” side by side.
    Fails if: most participants go straight to upload and succeed.

    H4

    The brief survives a council room

    Test: hand the printed brief to two people who've sat on a council; ask what they'd push back on.
    Fails if: the pushback is about things the brief could have answered.

    What I'd change first if H3 fails: inventory import from the tool cities already use. If H1 fails: ranges and sources on every estimate before anything else, because the whole product rests on it.

    How I'd measure it

    One north star: the brief reaches the meeting. Five events that explain it, with hypothetical targets so the numbers mean something from day one.

    Event (properties)What it tells meWhat I'd do with it
    inventory_completed (source: sample / manual)How people start, and whether manual entry loses themIf manual drops off, build import before anything else
    estimate_dragged (action, direction)How often users disagree, and which waySystematic drags in one direction mean the factor is wrong, not the user
    scenario_saved, scenario_switchedWhether comparison is real or decorativeLow use means the compare view should be a table, not a toggle
    brief_generated, brief_downloadedWhether the plan reaches the meetingGenerated but not downloaded means the brief isn't trusted yet
    step_abandoned (step, seconds)Where the 30-minute target breaksFix the slowest step first

    Guardrail: no personal data, no city identified without consent. Events carry the step and the action id, nothing else. Qualitative companion: a one-question survey after download, “What will the council push back on?”

    Where it sits, and what I'd build next

    Sources and ranges first, because the whole product rests on trust in the numbers.

    The gap in the market. Climate software for cities clusters around the inventory, the report and the analyst. Almost nothing is built for the officer's own decision, in one sitting. Inventory tools are the input; ClimatePath starts where they stop, which is why its design system comes from one of them.

    The math, simple on purpose. Impact share × sector emissions = tonnes avoided; × cost per tonne = rough cost, the dot's size; ÷ rollout years = the trajectory to 2030; summed against the target = the plan bar. Tonnes, not percent: a 35% cut of a small sector can matter less than a 6% cut of a big one, and tonnes are what the target is written in.

    Who else reads the brief. The officer needs a plan they can own: drag, undo, scenarios. The council needs four numbers and two options: the metrics strip, scenarios A and B. Finance needs cost, savings and payback: cost is there today, savings come next. Not answered yet: “the city doesn't control the buses” and “what's in it for residents?”

    Next, in order. A source, a range and a confidence on every estimate, because a single number without provenance is the first thing a councillor will attack. Co-benefit tags (air quality, jobs, bills) and a governance tag (“requires control of the transit operator”) on every action, because councils vote on those too. Savings and payback per action, so the finance director reads it without rewriting it. Then shared, versioned briefs with named owners, import from the inventory tool, Spanish for the many cities starting from zero in Latin America, and delivery tracking so the plan stays alive after the vote.

    What I learned

    • Data isn't the bottleneck; a defensible decision is. The most useful thing I built wasn't a chart. It was the moment the user could see a trade-off and explain it to someone else.
    • Building first changes what you design. With a working prototype on day seven, the undo, the quick wins and the “best next action” all came from using the tool, not from a wireframe.
    • Write the hypotheses before the screens. Four principles and four hypotheses did more for the product than any single feature.

    Try it yourself

    The prototype is live. Pick a sample city, build a plan, and draft the brief. It takes about five minutes.
