    Self-initiated · Unsolicited redesign

    MetaMask, Rethought for First-Time Users

    Crypto promises financial freedom. For a first-timer, MetaMask's first five minutes offer 40x leverage and sports predictions before they explain what a wallet is. I'm a crypto user and I love its philosophy, so I walked those five minutes the way a beginner meets them and redesigned them: protect first, then fund, then explore.

    Role
    Sole designer, end to end
    Type
    Unsolicited concept
    Platform
    MetaMask mobile, iOS
    Prototype
    Interactive, built with Claude
    Reading time
    6 minutes

    Unsolicited concept. I'm not affiliated with MetaMask or Consensys. Original screens were captured on iOS in October 2026; the redesign is my own proposal.

    The problem
    A new user creates a wallet without knowing what a wallet is, hits a $0 error when trying to add funds, and lands on 40x leverage and sports predictions before learning how to keep funds safe.
    What I did
    An expert walkthrough, reading each screen as a first-timer would, plus an audit against usability heuristics and behavioral science. Then a redesign of the first five minutes; users come next, in the test plan.
    The result
    A concept that puts protection, understanding and a first deposit ahead of trading, plus the metrics and the test plan I'd use to prove it.

    The hard call

    Safety before volume. Trading features are MetaMask's business, and moving them out of a new user's first screen could cost short-term volume. My bet is the opposite: people who understand and secure their wallet come back, and they trade for years. It's a hypothesis, and the test plan below is how I'd check it.

    Before and after, in four moments

    Tap a number to see what changed. Red marks what got in the way; green, how the redesign handles it.

    A choice made in the dark

    Before

    1. 1Three sign-in buttons, and no word on what each one means for who controls your funds.
    2. 2"Use Secret Recovery Phrase" looks like a fourth button, not a different way to own your wallet.
    redesign

    After

    1. 1One sentence explains what a wallet is: no bank in between, nobody can freeze it or recover it for you.
    2. 2Simple sign-in, recommended to start, with how you recover access.
    3. 3Recovery phrase, labeled "most control", with the responsibility stated plainly.

    Speculation on day one

    Before

    1. 1"Buy" next to every token, before you know how to receive or protect anything.
    2. 2Perpetuals with 40x leverage, shown to a wallet with $0.
    3. 3Sports predictions, one scroll away.
    redesign

    After

    1. 1$0.00 explained: "It's empty, which is normal."
    2. 2Setup in three steps: protect, get your address, add funds.
    3. 3Leverage and predictions wait until you have funds, labeled high risk.

    A dead end

    Before

    1. 1$0 in red and "No funds available. Use a different account." The first deposit starts as an error.
    2. 2"Select payment method" opened an empty list, with no reason.
    3. 310%, 25% and Max of $0.
    redesign

    After

    1. 1Every path shows its fee and time, and says when it isn't available in your country.
    2. 2Receive from a local exchange, with the exact network to use and your address.
    3. 3A warning before a wrong-network send can cost your funds.

    Urgency instead of safety

    Before

    1. 1A price alert, "ETH is up 4.2%", is the first thing a new wallet asks to send you.
    2. 2"Turn on notifications" before you have anything to be notified about.
    redesign

    After

    1. 1Fee in your currency and the total, before you confirm.
    2. 2The network checked against the address.
    3. 3"First time sending to this address": check it, sends can't be undone.
    4. 4Hold to send: a deliberate gesture for an irreversible action.

    Six moments of friction, and the fix for each

    I created a wallet with social sign-in and read every screen as a first-timer would, noting where they would stall. This is an expert walkthrough and a heuristic audit, not user research; the five-person test is in the plan at the end. Six findings stood out, each tied to the crypto mechanic underneath it, and each became a rule for the redesign.

    1. A key choice without information."Continue with Google" and "Use Secret Recovery Phrase" look like equal options, and nothing says who holds the key: social sign-in splits recovery across accounts; a recovery phrase puts it all on you. Fix: state that trade-off in one line before the choice.
    2. The most important warning, in the smallest type."MetaMask can't reset it" sits in small grey text, while a marketing opt-in gets a full card. Fix: teach at the moment of need: explain the 12 words right before showing them, with a one-question check, because fake "support" asks for exactly those words.
    3. Permission before value.Notifications are requested on the first screen, with an empty wallet, framed around price moves: "Never miss a move." Fix: ask once the first funds are on the way.
    4. A dead end as the first deposit."No funds available. Use a different account." in red, 10%, 25% and Max of $0, and an empty list of payment methods. Fix: never a dead end: every path shows its fee, its time and whether it works in your country, and receiving from an exchange names the network to use.
    5. Speculation before safety.An empty wallet shows 40x leverage, sports predictions with a live countdown and "top traders" up $58K to follow. Fix: protect, then fund, then explore; leverage and predictions wait until there are funds, labeled high risk.
    6. Overload on an empty wallet.Tokens, perps, predictions, a watchlist, traders and NFT imports on the first visit, but no clear balance or way to receive funds. Fix: a home that says the $0 is normal and guides setup: protect, get your address, add funds.

    The redesign

    Six screens cover the first five minutes and the first send. Same brand, same features; a different order, and explanation exactly where the fear is.

    The psychology behind itRetrieval practice. Answering one question about a scam protects people better than reading a warning. Recalling an idea is what makes it stick.Roediger and Karpicke, 2006

    Built for markets like Argentina

    In Argentina, crypto isn't a hobby. Many people use stablecoins to protect their savings from inflation, and a lot of them are first-time financial users. That changes the design: card on-ramps are often unavailable (in my walkthrough, the payment list came up empty), so receiving from a local exchange has to be a first-class path, not an afterthought; prices should be readable in the currency people think in; and every fee matters.

    Plain language, line by line

    Most of the redesign is words. A few before and after:

    BeforeAfter
    Use Secret Recovery PhraseRecovery phrase: you keep 12 secret words, and nobody can help if you lose them
    No funds available. Use a different account.Your wallet is empty, which is normal. Here's how to add your first funds.
    Never miss a moveWant us to tell you when your funds arrive?
    Perps · 40xTrading with leverage · High risk · Can lose more than you put in

    Prototype and proposed components

    I prototyped the whole flow in a day with Claude, so it can be clicked, tested and argued about, not just admired. It only uses data the wallet already has: the account type, the address format and the network fee estimate. Four patterns repeat across the screens, so I drew them up as a proposal for the design system.

    Try the prototype

    Six screens, clickable from the first sign-in to a hold-to-send confirmation.

    Open the prototype (opens in a new tab)

    How I'd prove it works

    A concept is a hypothesis until people use it. This is how I'd test it with MetaMask's team.

    • Usability test: five first-time crypto users, thinking aloud, current flow against the redesign. Can they explain what a wallet is, and fund it, without help?
    • A/B test on the first home: guided setup against the current feed, for new wallets only.
    • Metrics: wallets backed up in the first day, time to first deposit, share of new users who hit the $0 dead end, early support tickets about lost access, and 30-day retention.

    What I learned

    • Crypto doesn't need to be simpler than it is. It needs to be taught at the right moment, in the right order.
    • Self-custody is a promise and a responsibility. The design has to make both visible, without scaring people away.

    This is the work I want to do: help crypto keep its promise of financial freedom, starting with the people trying it for the first time.

    Self-initiated · Unsolicited redesign

    Verbier 4 Vallées: A Day Pass in Three Screens

    I bought a 4 Vallées day pass the way a first-time visitor would, and kept thinking of ways to make it easier. Nobody asked me to. There was no brief, no analytics and no research budget: the research was me, buying a pass the way a first-time visitor would, and checking every screen against e-commerce good practice, usability heuristics and what I know about cognitive load. The result takes five steps down to three screens, with the same products, prices and brand.

    Role
    Sole designer, end to end
    Type
    Unsolicited, not commissioned
    Research
    Myself as the user, plus heuristics and checkout practice
    Prototype
    Interactive, in English and French, built with Claude
    Reading time
    6 minutes

    Unsolicited redesign. I’m not affiliated with Téléverbier SA. The original screens come from the public shop on 20 October 2026; the redesign is my own concept, and the Verbier 4 Vallées name and logo belong to the resort.

    The problem
    Five steps to buy one pass, a price that changes between screens, an information button that erases your choice, and controls too small for a thumb.
    What I did
    Bought a pass as a first-time visitor would, logged thirteen findings with evidence, and redesigned the flow around fewer decisions per screen.
    The result
    Three screens before payment instead of five, every price where the decision is made, and three fixes that could ship in an afternoon.

    The hard call

    No numbers I couldn’t back. I don’t have the resort’s analytics, so this case promises no uplift. It shows what got in the way, what the redesign changes and why, and how the resort could measure it. Less spectacular, much harder to argue with.

    Before and after

    Five moments of the checkout: the shop as it was, next to the redesign. Tap a screen to see it larger.

    Choosing a sector

    Information that throws you out.

    Choosing a date

    A calendar that hides the price.

    Choosing passes

    A price that moves.

    Insurance

    A warning that scolds.

    Across every step: the header

    A countdown for something else.

    What I found, as a user

    I picked the flow most visitors take: one adult, one day, a Saturday in January, on my phone. I wrote down every moment I hesitated and every number that didn’t match, then checked each screen against usability heuristics, WCAG 2.2 and checkout practice. No interviews and no analytics: this is one expert user’s walkthrough, and the case says so.

    13 findings
    two of them critical, each backed by a quote from the shop or a measurement
    CHF 0.80
    between the price on the sector card and the price one screen later
    ≈16 px
    plus and minus buttons, below the 24 px WCAG 2.2 minimum and far from the 44 px touch guidance

    Two findings are critical because they lose customers who have already decided to buy: an unlabeled “i” that opens another page and erases the selection, and a price that reads CHF 73.00 on the card and CHF 73.80 one screen later. A number that moves reads like a hidden fee. The rest add friction right where people decide: a stepper that doesn’t describe the flow, information after the decision, a countdown for a different product, and buttons too small for a thumb.

    The psychology behind itThe curse of knowledge. Once you know the mountain, you forget what a first visit feels like. So I bought the pass as a visitor would, step by step, and wrote down every hesitation before my own knowledge filled the gaps.Camerer, Loewenstein and Weber, 1989

    Five improvements, and why

    Same products, same prices, same brand. What changes is how much a skier has to hold in mind between “I want to ski on Saturday” and “paid”.

    1. Three screens instead of five

      Sector and date share one screen; passes and insurance share one table; then a review, then payment.

      Why: Every extra step is a moment to leave, and every choice carried from one screen to the next is held in memory. Fewer, fuller screens mean fewer things to keep in mind.

      Cognitive load · Sweller, 1988

    2. The price where the decision is

      A price under every day in the calendar, and the same "from" price on the sector card and in the passes table.

      Why: People compare before they commit. A price shown at the point of choice removes the mental math, and a price that changes one screen later reads like a hidden fee.

      Checkout usability · Baymard Institute

    3. Buttons a thumb can hit

      Plus and minus at 44 px instead of about 16, and the total always in the bottom bar.

      Why: Small targets take longer to hit and get missed, on a phone most of all. Size and distance decide how fast and how surely people act.

      Fitts's law · Fitts, 1954

    4. Information in place, not on another page

      Sector details and insurance conditions open where you are and close with one tap.

      Why: Leaving the checkout to read something breaks the task and, in the original, erased the selection. Keeping it in place keeps the goal in view.

      Task interruption · Altmann and Trafton, 2002

    5. Words that inform instead of scold

      "No insurance, no refund!" became a neutral line about what each option covers. The stepper names each step, and the typo is gone.

      Why: Tone at the moment of paying shapes trust. A sentence that tells people off adds doubt exactly where they decide.

      Plain language · Nielsen Norman Group

    Three screens before paying

    Built as a clickable prototype with Claude, in English and French, so each change can be tried rather than imagined. Three of the fixes are copy and routing changes that could ship in an afternoon, before any redesign. Tap a screen to see it larger.

    How I’d measure it

    If the resort wanted to test it, I’d compare the old flow and the new one on the same weeks of the season:

    • Completion rate from the sector screen to payment, on phone and on desktop.
    • Drop-off on the date and passes steps, where the hidden prices and the small buttons live today.
    • Support tickets about prices and refunds.
    • Time from the first screen to payment.

    What I learned

    • Being a customer is research, with a caveat. Knowing the mountain told me what a first-time visitor needs before choosing a sector; walking the shop as that visitor showed me the friction I had stopped noticing.
    • Small words sit on big money. A typo in the stepper and a scolding line about insurance take an afternoon to fix, and they sit exactly where people decide to pay.
    • Fewer screens doesn’t mean less information. Each screen carries more, but every decision has what it needs right in front of it.

    Try the prototype

    Click through the redesign, switch between the original and the new screens, and read all thirteen findings, in English or French.

    This is how my mind works: when a ready customer hesitates, I want to take away the reason.

    Self-initiated · Restaurant menus

    Menu Redesigns: Better Choices at the Table

    I went out to dinner, read the menu and couldn't stop redesigning it in my head. That's how my mind works: I notice where information makes people work harder than they should. So I redesigned the menu of a four-star hotel restaurant without touching a single dish or price. Only the way the information is laid out. Then I did the same for the summer menu of La Table d'Adrien, a MICHELIN-starred restaurant.

    Role
    Sole designer: information design, behavioral design and content
    Deliverable
    Two redesigned printed menus and a dessert card
    Type
    Self-initiated, not commissioned
    Reading time
    5 minutes

    Personal exercises. Not commissioned by or affiliated with either restaurant. The hotel restaurant's name and logo are removed. La Table d'Adrien's dishes, prices and logo belong to the restaurant; the before photo is a guest's, published on Google Maps.

    The problem
    A hotel menu with one long column of prices and desserts decided before the first course; a starred restaurant whose menu online was a guest's photo of a stapled sheet.
    What I did
    Kept the kitchens' dishes and prices, and redesigned the hierarchy, the grouping, the wording and the order of the information.
    The result
    Menus that read in the order guests decide: which menu, which dishes, what to drink and, later, dessert.

    The hard call

    Change nothing on the plate. A redesign could have rewritten dishes or moved prices. In both menus I kept the kitchen's dishes and prices, so every improvement comes from information design alone, and the kitchen gives up nothing.

    Why a menu

    A menu is a decision tool that most restaurants treat as a list. Guests read it in a few minutes, often while talking, and it quietly decides what they order, what they pair it with and whether they stay for dessert.

    I love information that is placed with millimetric care. Good content direction is the kind you don't notice: the guest doesn't read a well designed menu, they simply choose.

    A hotel restaurant: before and after

    What changed, and why

    Six decisions, each grounded in how people read, compare and decide.

    1. Prices leave the column

      The price now closes each description instead of lining up on the right.

      Why: A column of numbers invites people to scan prices and compare them first. When the price follows the description, the dish is read before its cost.

      Menu engineering practice

    2. One Chef's Signature per section

      One framed dish per section, chosen by the kitchen.

      Why: With many similar options, people choose with less confidence. One highlighted dish gives the eye a place to start and the table a reference point.

      Choice overload · Iyengar and Lepper, 2000

    3. Three families of mains

      Eight mains in a row became three groups: from the land, from the sea, pasta and risotto.

      Why: Small groups are easier to hold in mind than a long list, so one big decision becomes two small ones.

      Chunking · Miller, 1956

    4. A suggested wine under every dish

      Each dish names one local wine, available by the glass, to be confirmed by the sommelier.

      Why: A sensible default makes the next decision easy while the choice stays open. Nobody has to face the whole wine list to order a glass.

      Choice architecture · Thaler and Sunstein, 2008

    5. Desserts arrive later

      Desserts moved to a small separate card that comes as the plates are cleared.

      Why: What we choose depends on how hungry we are when we choose. Decided before the first course, dessert is usually a no; decided at the end, it is a real choice.

      Read and van Leeuwen, 1998

    6. Two lines of story, and quiet details

      Two sentences set the scene. One logo, consistent capitals, a vegetarian mark and an allergy line that saves the staff questions.

      Why: Text that is easy to process feels more trustworthy and of higher quality. The guest never notices the details; they notice that the menu feels right.

      Processing fluency · Reber and Schwarz, 1999

    Content direction you don't notice

    The words do as much work as the layout, and they never announce themselves:

    • "Leave a little room: our dessert card follows your main course." One line at the bottom of the menu that keeps dessert in play without a hard sell.
    • "Every dish, its wine. Each pairing is available by the glass, simply ask." It removes the fear of committing to a bottle.
    • A vegetarian mark and one allergy line. The two questions staff hear most, answered on the page.

    A starred table: La Table d'Adrien

    La Table d'Adrien is the MICHELIN-starred restaurant of the Chalet d'Adrien hotel. Online, its menu was a guest's photo of a stapled sheet: an earlier tasting menu in one centered column. I redesigned the summer menu in the house identity, with the kitchen's own dishes and prices.

    1. Four menus, side by side

      The four tasting menus, from three to seven courses, sit in one row with their prices.

      Why: Options are easier to judge next to each other than one by one, and a longer menu beside a shorter one makes one more course feel natural. The price becomes a step, not a barrier.

      Compromise effect · Simonson, 1989

    2. The house on the page

      The logo, the Chef's name and the season open the menu, in the restaurant's own colors.

      Why: First impressions spill over onto what follows. A menu that looks like the house tells guests the evening is in good hands before the first plate.

      Halo effect · Thorndike, 1920

    3. Courses you can scan

      Dishes are grouped by course under small labels, with the name in a serif and the description below it.

      Why: People scan before they read. Clear labels and two levels of type let the eye jump from dish to dish instead of reading a column from top to bottom.

      How people read · Nielsen, 1997

    How I'd measure it

    Alternate the old and the new menu by night for four weeks, and compare:

    • Average check per guest, with dish prices unchanged.
    • Share of tables that order dessert, once the separate card arrives at the right moment.
    • Wine by the glass per dish, to see whether the suggested pairing gets ordered.
    • Time from seating to order, and how often staff are asked about allergens.

    This is where my two habits meet: noticing friction everywhere, and fixing it with information.
